extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and writers interested in literary theory (especially the fantastic)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying or composing texts in Todorov's sense of the 'fantastic': events that appear supernatural within a realistic world and provoke reader hesitation between natural and supernatural explanations. Useful for writers and analysts applying Todorov's genre criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic — basic condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The fantastic is any event that happens in our world that seems to be supernatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Todorov's basic diagnostic for the genre: the story presents an event occurring in a realistic, everyday world which appears to violate natural laws or to be supernatural. This is the starting point for further classification into uncanny, marvelous, or pure fantastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader hesitation / indecision (requirement for the fantastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the occurrence of the event, we must decide if the event was an illusion or whether it is real and has actually taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial to Todorov's definition is the response of the implied reader: the narrative must provoke a genuine hesitation between a natural (rational) explanation and a supernatural one. Only when the reader cannot opt for one interpretation over the other does the text qualify as purely 'fantastic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic uncanny (the rational/illusion interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the fantastic uncanny, the event that occurs is actually an illusion of some sort; the 'laws of reality' remain intact and provide a rational explanation for the fantastic event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Todorov lists examples of natural explanations that can dissolve the supernatural appearance: dreams, drugs, illusions of the senses, madness, etc. For writers: to place a text in the uncanny, provide an apparently supernatural occurrence but allow (or favor) a plausible rational account that preserves ordinary reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic marvelous (the supernatural-real interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the fantastic marvelous, the supernatural event that occurs has actually taken place and therefore the 'laws of reality' have to be changed to explain the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here the narrative endorses the supernatural reading: the text requires a revision of reality's laws to accommodate what happens. For writers, this entails committing the story-world to the reality of the supernatural occurrence rather than offering a rational explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure fantastic (indeterminacy as defining feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only if the implied reader cannot opt for one or the other possibility (rational vs. supernatural) is the text purely fantastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Todorov treats pure fantastic texts as those that deliberately maintain the interpretive instability — neither confirming nor denying the supernatural. This is a compositional strategy: sustain ambiguity, avoid decisive evidence, and keep interpretive cues balanced so readers remain undecided.
